misconceptions.statement: A cylinder has three faces, so a face means any surface including curved ones, and a sphere has one face.
misconceptions.why: Everyday word 'face' is used for any outer side.
misconceptions.fix: In NCERT usage a face is a flat surface; curved surfaces are called curved surfaces, not faces.

probe.question: How many flat faces does a sphere have?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Only the faces you can see in the picture exist on a solid.
misconceptions.why: Drawings show only three faces of a cube.
misconceptions.fix: A cube has six faces, including those hidden at the back, bottom and sides.

probe.question: A cube is drawn on paper showing three sides. How many faces does it have?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student spatial reasoning with 2D drawings of 3D objects

misconceptions.statement: An edge is any line drawn on the solid, including the boundary of a curved surface only if it is straight.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse edge with any line or side.
misconceptions.fix: An edge is the line segment where two faces of a solid meet.

probe.question: A cube has how many edges meeting at one corner?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: A vertex is any point on the solid, and a cone's curved top has no vertex.
misconceptions.why: Students link vertex only to square-like corners.
misconceptions.fix: A vertex is a corner point where edges meet; a cone has one vertex at its tip.

probe.question: How many vertices does a cone have?

misconceptions.root_belief: only typical examples count as the idea

misconceptions.statement: A triangular prism has 3 faces because its base is a triangle.
misconceptions.why: Students count sides of the base instead of all faces.
misconceptions.fix: A triangular prism has 2 triangular bases plus 3 rectangular faces, so 5 faces.

probe.question: How many faces does a triangular prism have?

misconceptions.root_belief: one part of an object represents the whole
misconceptions.source_hint: research on counting faces and edges of solids in geometry classrooms

misconceptions.statement: A prism with an n-sided base has n edges.
misconceptions.why: Students count only edges of the base.
misconceptions.fix: An n-sided prism has 3n edges: n on top, n on bottom and n joining them.

probe.question: How many edges does a pentagonal prism have?

misconceptions.root_belief: counting part of the thing gives the total

misconceptions.statement: A square pyramid has 4 faces because it has a square base with 4 sides.
misconceptions.why: Students forget to count the base as a face.
misconceptions.fix: A square pyramid has 4 triangular faces plus the square base, so 5 faces.

probe.question: How many faces does a square pyramid have?

misconceptions.root_belief: the base is not a real part

misconceptions.statement: A triangular pyramid has a triangular base and triangular sides, so it is named for its sides rather than its base.
misconceptions.why: Students see the lateral faces most prominently.
misconceptions.fix: A pyramid is named by the shape of its base; its side faces are always triangles.

probe.question: A pyramid with a hexagonal base has what shape of side faces and what is it called?

misconceptions.root_belief: the most visible part defines the whole

misconceptions.statement: A cylinder has no edges because it is round.
misconceptions.why: Students link edges only with straight lines.
misconceptions.fix: A cylinder has two curved edges where its flat circular faces meet the curved surface.

probe.question: How many edges does a cylinder have?

misconceptions.root_belief: an edge must be straight like a polygon's

misconceptions.statement: Any six squares joined together fold into a cube.
misconceptions.why: Students only check the count of squares.
misconceptions.fix: Only certain arrangements of six squares fold into a cube; there are 11 such nets. Some arrangements overlap.

probe.question: Six squares are in a 2 by 3 block. Will it fold into a cube?

misconceptions.root_belief: having the right parts means it works
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on students' spatial visualisation when folding nets of cubes

misconceptions.statement: A cube has only one net, the cross-shaped one.
misconceptions.why: The textbook shows one standard net.
misconceptions.fix: A cube has 11 different nets.

probe.question: How many different nets can a cube have?

misconceptions.root_belief: the first example shown is the only one
misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototype thinking in geometry

misconceptions.statement: The net of a cylinder is two circles and a rectangle whose length can be any size.
misconceptions.why: Students do not link the rectangle to the circle.
misconceptions.fix: The rectangle's length must equal the circumference of the circle so the sides meet when rolled.

probe.question: A cylinder has circles of radius 7 cm. Can a rectangle 10 cm long be its curved surface?

misconceptions.root_belief: parts of a figure are independent

misconceptions.statement: A net is the picture of the solid drawn in perspective.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse net with drawing of the solid.
misconceptions.fix: A net is a flat 2D pattern of all faces joined, which can be folded to make the solid.

probe.question: Is a drawing of a cube with three visible faces its net?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The front view, top view and side view of a solid always look the same.
misconceptions.why: Cube examples have identical views.
misconceptions.fix: Different directions can give different views; only symmetric solids like a cube give identical ones.

probe.question: A cuboid has dimensions 2, 3, 4. Are its top and front views identical?

misconceptions.root_belief: a special case holds for all cases
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' orthographic projection difficulties

misconceptions.statement: The top view of a cone is a triangle, as its side view is.
misconceptions.why: Students use the familiar side-on picture.
misconceptions.fix: A cone's top view is a circle with a centre point; only its side and front views are triangles.

probe.question: What is the top view of a cone?

misconceptions.root_belief: an object looks the same from every side

misconceptions.statement: A view of stacked cubes shows how many cubes there are in total.
misconceptions.why: Students count squares in a view as cubes.
misconceptions.fix: A view shows only one side; hidden cubes behind or below must be inferred, so the count of squares can differ from the cubes in the solid.

probe.question: The front view of a block structure shows 4 squares. How many cubes does it have?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' interpretation of isometric and orthogonal drawings of cube buildings

misconceptions.statement: A vertical slice of a cylinder always gives a circle.
misconceptions.why: Students picture the circular top.
misconceptions.fix: A slice parallel to the base is a circle, but a vertical slice through the axis is a rectangle.

probe.question: A cylinder is cut straight down along its axis. What shape is the cut face?

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar view stands for all views
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student understanding of cross-sections of solids

misconceptions.statement: The shadow of a solid is the same shape as the solid.
misconceptions.why: Students think shadows copy objects.
misconceptions.fix: A shadow is a 2D shape that depends on the light direction; a cube can cast a square or a hexagon.

probe.question: A ball is lit from above. What shape is its shadow?

misconceptions.root_belief: a copy looks exactly like the original

misconceptions.statement: Euler's formula is F + V + E = 2.
misconceptions.why: Students misremember the sign of E.
misconceptions.fix: Euler's formula is F + V - E = 2.

probe.question: A cube has 6 faces, 8 vertices, 12 edges. Check Euler's formula.

misconceptions.root_belief: all quantities in a formula add

misconceptions.statement: To find edges using Euler's formula, E = F + V + 2.
misconceptions.why: Students rearrange the formula without changing signs.
misconceptions.fix: From F + V - E = 2 we get E = F + V - 2.

probe.question: A solid has 5 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges?

misconceptions.root_belief: moving a term across keeps its sign
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors in transposing terms in equations

misconceptions.statement: Euler's formula works for every solid, including a cylinder or cone.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the rule to everything.
misconceptions.fix: Euler's formula is for polyhedra with flat faces and straight edges only.

probe.question: A cone has 2 faces, 1 vertex, 1 edge. Does F + V - E = 2?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 2 + 1 - 1 = 2, so it holds for all solids

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule works everywhere once learned

misconceptions.statement: A cylinder is a polyhedron since it has flat circular faces.
misconceptions.why: Flat faces are noticed without the polygon requirement.
misconceptions.fix: A polyhedron needs all faces to be flat polygons; a cylinder has a curved surface so it is not one.

probe.question: Is a cylinder a polyhedron?

misconceptions.root_belief: one matching feature means the same category

misconceptions.statement: Any solid with a rectangular face is a prism.
misconceptions.why: Prisms are remembered by their rectangular sides.
misconceptions.fix: A prism has two identical parallel bases joined by rectangular faces; a pyramid can have rectangular base without being a prism.

probe.question: A rectangular-based pyramid has a rectangle face. Is it a prism?

misconceptions.root_belief: one matching feature means the same category
